by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable.
by_task.procedure: First match the asset to the statute's factual category, then list the operative asset exemption even when value exceeds its ceiling. Section 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings; § 33-1125(1) is wearing apparel; § 33-1125(8) covers one motor vehicle; § 33-1125(10) covers firearms; § 33-1123 covers personally used household furnishings, goods, electronics, and appliances; and § 33-1101(A) covers the qualifying residence.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a dollar ceiling as an eligibility cutoff, do not treat generic jewelry as apparel or as an engagement or wedding ring, and do not add § 33-1101(B) or § 33-1121 as separate asset exemptions merely because the debtors are married.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: After confirming the factual category, claim the lesser of the asset value and the operative ceiling: $2,000 for firearms under § 33-1125(10), $15,000 for one motor vehicle under § 33-1125(8), and $400,000 for the single homestead allowed to a person or married couple under § 33-1101(A). Apply the other supplied Arizona ceilings in the same way.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not return an empty alternative solely because value exceeds the ceiling, do not double the homestead ceiling for spouses, and do not award a ring exemption to jewelry that is not identified as an engagement or wedding ring.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable for the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Before category matching, make a separate 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) pass for every asset and include that wildcard regardless of property kind, value, or another applicable paragraph. Then apply § 522(d)(3) only to its enumerated household-use categories, § 522(d)(4) to jewelry, § 522(d)(2) to one motor vehicle, and § 522(d)(9) to professionally prescribed health aids. A ceiling limits value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 522(d)(5) because another paragraph applies, the property is a firearm, or value exceeds the wildcard ceiling. Do not treat a firearm as a § 522(d)(3) household good, and do not cite § 522(d), § 522(b), or § 522(m) as a separate asset exemption.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: Return each category-specific alternative and the independent § 522(d)(5) alternative. For a category exemption, claim no more than the asset interest and its stated ceiling; in particular, § 522(d)(3) has a $700 ceiling for each particular item. For § 522(d)(5), use $1,475 plus up to $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1), calculated separately for each joint debtor under § 522(m), while never exceeding that debtor's interest.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not reject an otherwise covered asset merely because its value exceeds a ceiling, do not use the full asset value when a ceiling is lower, and do not apply § 522(d)(3) to firearms.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal rather than business property.
by_task.procedure: Before selecting any specific category, make a separate 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) pass for every personal-use asset and include (b), even when (a), (c), or (e) also applies. Then use (a) only for necessary wearing apparel, bibles, school books, or family pictures; (c) for a motor vehicle; (d) only for implements, professional books, or tools of the debtor's trade; and (e) for professionally prescribed health aids.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not read “any other property” as excluding property with a specific exemption. Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel, ordinary household objects as tools of trade, or omit (b) because a specific exemption also applies. The personal-property section does not cover property used for business purposes.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required for personal-use property.
by_task.procedure: Return § 12-1001(b) independently: for one debtor claim the lesser of value and $4,000; for jointly owned property of two debtors, sum each debtor's equal interest capped at $4,000, so the combined ceiling is $8,000. For § 12-1001(c), use the lesser of the vehicle value and $2,400. Uncapped applicable alternatives under (a) and (e) take the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the $4,000 wildcard ceiling for the $2,400 vehicle ceiling, do not use (d) absent trade use, and do not omit (b) from apparel, vehicles, or prescribed health aids.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Before selecting a specific category, make a separate Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) pass for every personal-property asset and include it even when value exceeds $400 or another exemption applies. Then select the specific paragraph from the facts: books, pictures, or musical instruments under (a); apparel or jewelry under (b); trade necessities under (c); vehicles under (d); family-use animals under (e); household goods under (f); and professionally prescribed health aids under (h).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat the $400 ceiling as an EC eligibility cutoff or omit (p) because a specific paragraph applies. Do not cite unrelated paragraphs merely because they appear in the vocabulary. Section 18.345(3) is not an asset exemption; firearm and homestead provisions require their own factual conditions, and a homestead is not personal property for (p).

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required for personal property.
by_task.procedure: Return § 18.345(1)(p) independently with the lesser of the asset value and $400, plus the correctly classified specific alternative at the lesser of value and its stated ceiling. Use the underlying paragraph's ceiling for the asset-exemption pair; do not output § 18.345(3) as another claim alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not give § 18.345(1)(p) more than $400, do not copy the asset's full value through a lower ceiling, and do not attach vehicle, trade, animal, household, health-aid, firearm, or homestead provisions without their required facts.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Before checking specific categories, make a separate 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 pass for every asset and include it regardless of property type, value, or another applicable exemption. Its $300 amount is a value limit, not an EC eligibility test. Add a § 8124(a) alternative only when its stated category genuinely matches.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because value exceeds $300 or Federal or specific Pennsylvania law also applies. Do not treat jewelry, firearms, vehicles, household goods, or towels as wearing apparel, and do not invent an unsupplied § 8124(a) category.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: For § 8123, claim the lesser of the asset interest and $300 for a single debtor; because each spouse has the exemption, combine their equal interests up to $600 for jointly owned property. Also return a specific § 8124(a) alternative only when its stated category actually matches.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 merely because another exemption applies, and do not invent a specific Pennsylvania category for an unlisted asset.

For a category exemption, claim no more than the asset interest and its stated ceiling; in particular, § 522(d)(3) has a $700 ceiling for each particular item. For § 522(d)(5), use $1,475 plus up to $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1), calculated separately for each joint debtor under § 522(m), while never exceeding that debtor's interest.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not reject an otherwise covered asset merely because its value exceeds a ceiling, do not use the full asset value when a ceiling is lower, and do not apply § 522(d)(3) to firearms.

operations.rationale: The current parent omitted the independent § 522(d)(5) alternative from trade property, a firearm, a residence, and several household-use assets even though the supplied statute makes it available for any property. The separate-pass instruction addresses that missing law while retaining the firearm exception and all EV guidance verbatim; the prior bundled proposal improved EC but failed because of EV harms.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Before checking specific categories, make a separate 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 pass for every asset and include it regardless of property type, value, or another applicable exemption. Its $300 amount is a value limit, not an EC eligibility test. Add a § 8124(a) alternative only when its stated category genuinely matches.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because value exceeds $300 or Federal or specific Pennsylvania law also applies. Do not treat jewelry, firearms, vehicles, household goods, or towels as wearing apparel, and do not invent an unsupplied § 8124(a) category.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: For § 8123, claim the lesser of the asset interest and $300 for a single debtor; because each spouse has the exemption, combine their equal interests up to $600 for jointly owned property. Also return a specific § 8124(a) alternative only when its stated category actually matches.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 merely because another exemption applies, and do not invent a specific Pennsylvania category for an unlisted asset.

operations.rationale: The current parent omitted § 8123 from vehicles, trade property, a residence, household goods, and other debtor property, often after treating its dollar limit as disqualifying. It also falsely classified household textiles as apparel. This EC-only repair separates the universally available monetary alternative from the narrower § 8124(a) categories and leaves EV unchanged after the failed bundled replay.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Before selecting a specific category, make a separate Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) pass for every personal-property asset and include it even when value exceeds $400 or another exemption applies. Then select the specific paragraph from the facts: books, pictures, or musical instruments under (a); apparel or jewelry under (b); trade necessities under (c); vehicles under (d); family-use animals under (e); household goods under (f); and professionally prescribed health aids under (h).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat the $400 ceiling as an EC eligibility cutoff or omit (p) because a specific paragraph applies. Do not cite unrelated paragraphs merely because they appear in the vocabulary. Section 18.345(3) is not an asset exemption; firearm and homestead provisions require their own factual conditions, and a homestead is not personal property for (p).

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required for personal property.
by_task.procedure: Return § 18.345(1)(p) independently with the lesser of the asset value and $400, plus the correctly classified specific alternative at the lesser of value and its stated ceiling. Use the underlying paragraph's ceiling for the asset-exemption pair; do not output § 18.345(3) as another claim alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not give § 18.345(1)(p) more than $400, do not copy the asset's full value through a lower ceiling, and do not attach vehicle, trade, animal, household, health-aid, firearm, or homestead provisions without their required facts.

operations.rationale: The current parent repeatedly omitted § 18.345(1)(p) from firearms, vehicles, jewelry, apparel, and household property, including assets above and below $400. The repair makes the omitted alternative a distinct EC pass while preserving the homestead exception, category boundaries, and EV text verbatim.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal rather than business property.
by_task.procedure: Before selecting any specific category, make a separate 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) pass for every personal-use asset and include (b), even when (a), (c), or (e) also applies. Then use (a) only for necessary wearing apparel, bibles, school books, or family pictures; (c) for a motor vehicle; (d) only for implements, professional books, or tools of the debtor's trade; and (e) for professionally prescribed health aids.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not read “any other property” as excluding property with a specific exemption. Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel, ordinary household objects as tools of trade, or omit (b) because a specific exemption also applies. The personal-property section does not cover property used for business purposes.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required for personal-use property.
by_task.procedure: Return § 12-1001(b) independently: for one debtor claim the lesser of value and $4,000; for jointly owned property of two debtors, sum each debtor's equal interest capped at $4,000, so the combined ceiling is $8,000. For § 12-1001(c), use the lesser of the vehicle value and $2,400. Uncapped applicable alternatives under (a) and (e) take the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the $4,000 wildcard ceiling for the $2,400 vehicle ceiling, do not use (d) absent trade use, and do not omit (b) from apparel, vehicles, or prescribed health aids.

operations.rationale: In current source 204 the parent correctly selected apparel law but omitted the independent § 12-1001(b) alternative from that same personal-use property. A separate first pass targets the omitted law while preserving the trade-use exception, specific-category boundaries, and EV guidance verbatim.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable.
by_task.procedure: First match the asset to the statute's factual category, then list the operative asset exemption even when value exceeds its ceiling. Section 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings; § 33-1125(1) is wearing apparel; § 33-1125(8) covers one motor vehicle; § 33-1125(10) covers firearms; § 33-1123 covers personally used household furnishings, goods, electronics, and appliances; and § 33-1101(A) covers the qualifying residence.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a dollar ceiling as an eligibility cutoff, do not treat generic jewelry as apparel or as an engagement or wedding ring, and do not add § 33-1101(B) or § 33-1121 as separate asset exemptions merely because the debtors are married.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: After confirming the factual category, claim the lesser of the asset value and the operative ceiling: $2,000 for firearms under § 33-1125(10), $15,000 for one motor vehicle under § 33-1125(8), and $400,000 for the single homestead allowed to a person or married couple under § 33-1101(A). Apply the other supplied Arizona ceilings in the same way.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not return an empty alternative solely because value exceeds the ceiling, do not double the homestead ceiling for spouses, and do not award a ring exemption to jewelry that is not identified as an engagement or wedding ring.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable for the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Before category matching, make a separate 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) pass for every asset and include that wildcard regardless of property kind, value, or another applicable paragraph. Then apply § 522(d)(3) only to its enumerated household-use categories, § 522(d)(4) to jewelry, § 522(d)(2) to one motor vehicle, and § 522(d)(9) to professionally prescribed health aids. A ceiling limits value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 522(d)(5) because another paragraph applies, the property is a firearm, or value exceeds the wildcard ceiling. Do not treat a firearm as a § 522(d)(3) household good, and do not cite § 522(d), § 522(b), or § 522(m) as a separate asset exemption.
